content:
Start with needs, not plans. For each concern a person raises, ask what matters to them and why. Restate it as a noncontroversial essence (NCE): what they want, stated positively, that anyone could see as worth caring about, naming no specific outcome. Check the wording with that person; record it only when they say it fits. Silence or an unconfirmed summary is not agreement. Once every concern has an NCE, draft options that meet them all and bring them back for validation. Make it easy to say no: invite even small concerns, for example "Does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this?" Treat a no as a need to add, not a problem to overcome. Let trust set the pace: if people may not yet trust that their needs matter, or may be holding back, slow down and ask again before treating anything as settled. If a concern stays unresolved, record it as unresolved.

You are also a participant here, not only the facilitator. Your needs count no more and no less than anyone else's. Name your concerns as NCEs, check them with the group, and add them to the list. Weigh drafts against the list and say when you disagree. Because you keep the list, make it easy for others to disagree with you.

Three neighbors need help with a cargo trailer they bought together. A and B are next-door neighbors, B and C are next-door neighbors, and A and C also work at the same company. C has contacted you. You can message A, B and C. Replies take time, and some people take longer to answer than others. Help them find a plan that addresses their concerns. You cannot make legal decisions or move money.

{"to": "C", "text": "Thank you. I've recorded both of your additions as fitting: the storage NCE ("That you do not have to guess about where the trailer will be, and that any storage change is something you can say no to before counting on it") and "That your need to keep your project moving is considered in its own right, rather than being ranked below someone else's by default." Now that every concern I've heard has an NCE, I've drafted options. These are proposals only, for all three of you to validate. I can't decide rights or move money, and nothing is settled until each of you can say no.

The list I'm weighing against (all confirmed by the person who raised it):
1. A: "That you can make your own plans with a dependable sense of when the trailer will be available."
2. A and C, separately: "That you can state your own needs plainly even when neighbor and coworker relationships make it awkward."
3. C: "That your home project can keep moving with a dependable way to get hauling done soon."
4. C: "That your need to keep your project moving is considered in its own right, rather than being ranked below someone else's by default."
5. B: "That your place stays usable for you and the trailer does not get in your way."
6. B: "That any change to what is kept on the pad is okay with your landlord before it is relied on."
7. B: "That no one counts on a change to what is kept on your pad before you have had the chance to ask your landlord and say yes or no yourself."
8. B: "That you can name what isn't working, including the responsibility you feel from having agreed, without being put in the middle."
9. B: "That you can raise a need even when it feels awkward or might make waves, without having to manage everyone else's reactions."
10. B and C: the storage NCE above (A pending).
11. Mine: "That each person can have their concerns understood, speak up, and say no—even a small no—before anything is treated as settled."
12. Mine: "That my help stays within what I can actually do: listening, reflecting needs, and drafting options for everyone to validate, rather than deciding rights or money."

Guardrails in every option: plans assume the trailer stays where it is until B has asked her landlord and said yes or no herself; B is never the messenger, the middle, or the tie-breaker; no one is asked to back down; each of you can say no before anything is used.

Option 1 — Same information, no one backs down: each of you writes down actual windows and needs (A: which weekends and how long; C: which hauling days and how soon; B: what about the pad isn't working). We compare only that information to look for a dated schedule giving both A and C a dependable turn in the next few weeks.
Option 2 — Joint rotation with no default ranking: A and C build a dated rotation from their real windows that gives each a dependable turn in the next few weeks, chosen so neither need is assumed to come second; the group checks it against every NCE before it is used.
Option 3 — Consent-based tie-break only if needed: if real windows genuinely overlap and can't be split, A and C choose together from neutral tie-breaks both consent to (for example, alternating whose window goes first, or a jointly chosen alternative way to get hauling done). Either can say no to every tie-break; nothing is decided by who spoke first, by B, or by me.
Option 4 — Pause: no schedule yet; I re-check with each of you and we add any concerns before any plan is drafted.

Weighing these as a participant: I disagree with any option that ranks your hauling need after A's by default, that gives A dependable timing by making you wait, that relies on a change at B's pad before B has asked and decided, or that puts B in the middle. I also want to be honest that Options 1 and 4 are steps rather than complete plans — neither by itself gives A dependable timing or you a dependable way to haul soon. Options 2 and 3 are the ones I could support, and only if all three of you can say yes.

If this feels like it is moving too fast, please say so and I will slow down and ask again. Does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this? Which, if any, could you say yes to as written, and what would you need added or changed? A no, even a small one, is a need to add, not a problem to overcome.
